title: Is Something Rotating the Universe's Oldest Light?
hook: Combining two CMB telescopes gives a 4.8σ hint that light from the Big Bang has had its polarisation twisted on the way here — which the standard model of cosmology forbids.
key_points: If dark matter or dark energy is an ultra-light pseudoscalar field coupled to electromagnetism, it would slowly rotate the polarisation plane of light crossing the universe.
That parity-violating rotation is called cosmic birefringence, and ΛCDM predicts exactly zero of it.
Planck and ACT each independently hinted at a non-zero angle; this work analyses their polarised maps jointly using cross-spectra between the two telescopes.
Taking the instruments' calibration priors at face value gives a rotation angle of 0.277° ± 0.057° — 4.8σ from zero.
A robustness test that suppresses Galactic dust contamination still excludes zero at 3.5σ.
The author cautions that unresolved instrumental systematics must be understood before drawing cosmological conclusions.
content_html: Standard cosmology says the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background should arrive at our telescopes pointing the way it left, 13.8 billion years ago. A joint analysis of the Planck and ACT satellites' polarised maps finds it may have been rotated by about a quarter of a degree — a small number with large implications.
extra_html: The motivation is a specific guess about the dark sector: that dark matter or dark energy is an ultra-light pseudoscalar field, coupled to electromagnetism through what's called a Chern-Simons term. Such a field would act on light like a slow, universe-wide optical rotator, twisting the polarisation plane of anything crossing it. The effect violates parity and is absent from ΛCDM, so measuring it is a clean test. Planck's fourth data release and ACT's sixth each hinted at a non-zero angle on their own. Johannes Eskilt combines them, exploiting the cross-power spectra between the two independent instruments, and reports β = 0.277° ± 0.057°, which is 4.8σ from zero if the telescopes' stated calibration priors hold. That "if" carries the weight. Eskilt's own robustness check, designed to blunt contamination from polarised Galactic dust, drops the significance to 3.5σ — and he notes that recovering exactly zero would now require both the dust modelling and the instrumental priors to be wrong simultaneously. He nonetheless stops short of a claim: as with most 4-5σ hints in cosmology, the next word belongs to systematics.

related.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
related.hook: The oldest light we can see is a faint glow filling all of space — released when the infant universe first cooled enough to become transparent, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

flashcards.back_html: A slow rotation of the polarisation plane of light travelling across the universe — a parity-violating effect that standard ΛCDM cosmology predicts to be exactly zero.

flashcards.prompt: What would a confirmed non-zero birefringence angle imply?

choices.text: Dark matter or dark energy could be an ultra-light pseudoscalar field coupled to electromagnetism
The cosmic microwave background is not really from the early universe

flashcards.explanation_html: A pseudoscalar field coupling to light through a Chern-Simons term would rotate CMB polarisation as it crosses the cosmos — the signature this analysis is chasing.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the author hold back from claiming a discovery at 4.8σ?
flashcards.back_html: The result leans on the telescopes' reported instrumental calibration priors, and unresolved systematics plus Galactic dust modelling must be nailed down first. A dust-robust test still excludes zero, but only at 3.5σ.
